utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the 23rd, the Chamber had read out an order on exhibits, book evidence exhibits, and after some discussion expunged the order for further consideration of the submissions that were made by counsel. The order has now been redrafted, and it reads as follows. 1. Each party shall indicate which pages of the three books it wishes to keep on the record by Friday, the 2nd of June, 2006. 2. Each party shall properly scan only the B/C/S portions and corresponding English portions which it wishes to keep on the record and resubmit them to the registrar by Friday, the 2nd of June, 2006. 3. The registrar shall correct the trial record accordingly and assign any new exhibit numbers necessary out of court. Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll certainly comply with that order, as with all orders. Ms. Valabhji will be handling the next witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls it's next witness, John McElligott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: John?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: McElligott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make -- take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may take your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Please stationary for the court.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: My name is John McElligott, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Since we'll both be speaking English, please leave a short pause after my questions, so as to facilitate the work of the interpreters. Mr. McElligott, are you of Irish nationality and were you born in 1945?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: After completing your secondary education, did you join the Irish police force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What positions did you hold in the Irish police force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I joined originally as a -- what would be regarded as the rank of constable. I was promoted to an inspector sergeant, to an inspector, and to a detective superintendent.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: When did you retire from the police force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I retired in April of the year 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you at certain points in your career perform duties with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Please tell us about these duties in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: My first term with the United Nations was in Namibia, and that was during the years 1988 and 1989. I worked there for a period of 13 months.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: With what organisation were you affiliated in Namibia.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: The mission was known as UNTAG, that is the United Nations Transition Assistance Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what position did you told with UNTAG?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I was attached to the UNPROFOR -- UNCIVPOL headquarters and I held the position as head of communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you at some point thereafter work for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, what does UNPROFOR stand for.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: The United Nations Transition Assistance Group in the Former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Where were you based when you were with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I was based at the CIVPOL headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What did CIVPOL stand for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: It is the civilian police component of the UN commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you in more detail about UNPROFOR and UNCIVPOL. First, why was UNPROFOR established?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was established under the Vance Plan, and its concept was that the United Nations troops and police force would enter certain areas of Croatia, known as United Nations protected areas. These were generally referred to UNPAs, UNPAs. The area was to be demilitarised. Military forces were to withdraw or disband, and the UNPROFOR military forces were to ensure the safety of the area and that it would remain demilitarised. The civilian police component was to monitor the activities of the local police. It was also envisaged that the parties would engage in discussions and agree to co-exist within the area of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: When was UNPROFOR established in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: It was due to commence in February of 19 -- or 19 -- I forget my years. My apologies. 1988, sorry. I was there in -- let me just my bearings on time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Take your time, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Apologies. I served between 2000 -- I've forgotten my years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1998, yes. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Was it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, did you say 1990 or 1998 when you corrected yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you refer -- I mentioned my period of service in -- with UNPROFOR, so if you could refer me back to that. I just have ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sure. Did you work with UNPROFOR between October 1992 and October 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yeah. The mission was to commence in February of 1992 - my apologies - and I understand it did not take fill effect in Sector East and May and Sector West in June and Sectors North and South in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: We'll return to the topic of the sectors later. Now, I just want to clarify something. Earlier when you talked about your work with UNTAG in Namibia, you mentioned that the acronym UNTAG stands for UN Transitional Assistance Group. Now, the acronym UNPROFOR, is that the same thing or is that something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: It's the United Nations Protection Force within the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we are on the question of defining terms, what is the Vance Plan and what does it entail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vance Plan -- the concept was that the United Nations troops and police components would enter an area of Croatia known as United Nations protected areas, and the boundaries of that were set out in accordance with the Vance Plan. And the area was to be demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the Vance Plan was the plan that provided for entry of United Nations forces into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'd now like to go through some documents pertaining to UNCIVPOL functions and structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could the document with ERN 03630803 please be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a page from the standard operating procedures that we had, UNCIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could the page be enlarged a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a page from the UNCIVPOL operating procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's scroll down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the signature in the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I do, it's mine, and the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's scroll to the middle of the page. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What was the mandate of UNCIVPOL, according to this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: "To monitor the local police, to ensure that they carry out their tasks without discrimination on any grounds of ethnic origin, culture, religion, sex, or nationality, and with full respect for the human rights of all residents of the mission area." And secondly: "To provide appropriate assistance to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the International committee of Red Cross (ICRC) or other UNPROFOR-recognised humanitarian agencies, in support of their work to facilitate the return, in conditions of safety and security, of citizens -- or civilians who have been displaced by the conflict."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And just to be clear on terminology, were the UN monitors referred to as UN civilian police monitors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's scroll further down the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is UN civil police monitors, are they the same thing as UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's turn to the next page. Could we -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, could you summarise for us the monitoring functions of UNCIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Our function was to monitor them, the police, and that entailed observing them conducting their investigations, how they dealt with prisoners in the course of their detention, people who were arrested, houses being searched. We accompanied them to the scenes of crime. We accompanied them on patrols to see how they carry out their duties. We also conducted our own patrols to monitor their visibility, or the lack of it, and to establish what was happening in communities. We assisted in humanitarian issues with the various agencies of the United Nations, including the Red Cross and the commissioner for refugees. We also made reports on incidents, as they came to our notice, and on occasions we would have carried out our own inquiries to establish the credibility of some issues. We also made reports on other matter coming to our notice. Our monitors act as, I suppose, facilitators in conflict, particularly within the communities, and they engaged in many humanitarian issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence and assigned an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 721, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: We've just talked about the mandate and monitoring functions of UNCIVPOL. Who had the primary responsibility for maintaining law and order in the mission area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: That was the responsibility of the local police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, did the UN civilian police have executive powers or responsibility for maintaining public order?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Were the UN civilian police monitors armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could document 03630807 please be shown.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the second microphone of the witness be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness -- thank you, that's great. Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: It is the organisation chart for the CIVPOL organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe the UNCIVPOL's structure using this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: The structure was one where the commissioner had overall authority of the civilian police component. And at headquarters he had two assistants -- if you can enlarge --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I think we have the B/C/S on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we return to the English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was Chief of Staff who had primary responsibility for the personnel and logistical matters relating to the force. And the second was a deputy commissioner who had responsibility for operational matters. The commissioner or the UNPROFOR police force was divided into what are known as sectors, and they are shown there as Sectors North, South, East, West, and you have Sarajevo and sector -- I'm not sure of the area it actually covers. It doesn't come to me. But each of those sector commanders were responsible to the commissioner. In other words, the line of command was from the commissioner to the sector chiefs in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature at the bottom right-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is document 722.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I was chief of operations and I then transferred over to Chief of Staff for a period and then back to deputy commission at the latter end of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And could you briefly tell us what -- pardon me. I withdraw that question. Now, the document we just looked at mentions Sectors North, South, East, and West. With this in mind, let's take a look at 03630808. There seems to be some difficulty in retrieving the document. This document should be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Valabhji, do you, by any chance, have hard copies of the document? Enough to go around, if you do?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I think we have a few copies -- oh, I see. I think we just have one clean copy, unfortunately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. We just have to find it in e-court then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are certain it does exist in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: It is -- it is in e-court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. I think it's on its way. There we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: This document sets out the CIVPOL stations at the various sectors. It's showing the sector headquarters at the top line, and underneath for the stations in respect of each sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Where was Sector South based?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Sector South headquarters was based at Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what about Sector North, where was --

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Sector North was based at Topusko.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence and assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask a question before we assign a number to it? That's fine. I don't have to -- I don't have a question to ask. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit Number 723, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the document bearing ERN 0600 3593 please be shown. It is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, did you provide this map or sketch to the OTP earlier this week?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What does this map or sketch portray?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: The coloured area sets out the United Nations protected areas, and they are displayed in red.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Is it accurate, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I understand it to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you point out the various sectors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Sector East --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you get to that point, did you draw this map yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, Your Honour. It was one provided sometime during the mission period, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who provided it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have come from somewhere within the mission staffing level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I think there's a pen marker that can be utilised.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: If I could refer the court just to a note on the top right-hand corner, it does give some reference to it and I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on that note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says here it is not an official sketch produced by the UNMOs, they are the military observers at the headquarters. So it would be drafted by the military component of the military observers. So that is the source of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the military component of the UN?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we now return to the full -- that is, to zoom out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I was -- didn't express myself clearly. What I meant was for the full picture to be displayed again and for the zooming-in function to be negated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Using this pen, could you point out the various sectors.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Sector East is the area I am now circling.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And the remaining sectors.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Sector West is the next one here. And Sector North and south are joined, but the dividing boundary is somewhere here. I'm not exactly sure on it, but I recognise that one station is in Sector South, Korenica, and the next one is in Sector North. So the boundary lies somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, let's scroll down to the bottom left-hand corner, please. Thank you for informing me about that. Could the picture please be saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it at all possible to get the document occupying the entire screen and make it a little bigger, zoom in or out or whatever you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the document to make it a bit bigger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it is possible. Ms. Valabhji wanted the bottom, left corner, so if you can perhaps show that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is the date on this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: It is dated the 17th of April, 1993, that's 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I wonder if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but on my monitor I am not getting the map, I am getting OTP counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could the marked-up exhibit please be admitted into evidence and assigned an exhibit number. It's no longer on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: The map I have right now is the unmarked one. I think the one the witness marked has been saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. May the document on which the witness made markings, the saved map, please be admitted into -- be given an exhibit number, and it is hereby admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map will be Exhibit Number 724, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And the last in this particular series of documents, not the last document today but the last in the series, 03630809. Could this document please be exhibited. Sir, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: It is a profile of the staff and the station commanders at the various sectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on the right-hand side of the page?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 3 of the document. Could we zoom in, and could we scroll down, please. That suffices, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, how many monitors were there in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Sector North had 187, that's 187 -- or 167 -- it's not exactly clear here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we zoom in a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Just to verify that we looked at Sector North, could we scroll back up to the top of the page, please. Okay. Thank you. Could we now turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What sector does this page pertain to?
This sets out the profile for Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How many monitors were there?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour could this document please be admitted into evidence and assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 725, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Earlier we discussed the monitoring functions of UNCIVPOL. Was there a reporting procedure within UNCIVPOL?
Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What was the reporting procedure?

The reporting procedure was that a daily situation was prepared every 24 hours, each evening. And the procedure was that police monitors at the end of their day submitted their report to their respective station commanders. At station level a situation report was prepared, setting out all incidents coming to notice in that station throughout the day. That report was then sent to the sector chiefs' headquarters. So each station submitted a report to its sector chief, and at sector headquarters a member staff there prepared an overall situation report, reflecting the activities of the entire sector. That was then sent by each sector chief to the headquarters at Zagreb. A member of staff at my office then, during the course of the night, prepared an overall report setting out the overall position in the entire mission for the previous 24 hours. That report was then available to the commissioner and his key staff for their meeting in the morning. It was also circulated to the head of civil affairs or the director of civil affairs and to the force commander. And the various sector chiefs' reports would be available to the head of civil affairs at the sector headquarters as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: You mentioned the CIVPOL commissioner. To whom did he report?
He reported to the force commander through the director of civil affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what were the functions of the director of civil affairs?
Civil affairs director, I suppose, was to manage or direct all the political and civil affairs of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Finally, were there meetings with sector chiefs at CIVPOL headquarters?
Yes. There were regular meetings with the sector chiefs. These were, I believe, held once a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what would these have been about -- what were they about?

They mainly focussed on our operations on the ground, and we reviewed our performance and the operational activities on the ground and, I suppose, warfare [sic] strategies and how to deal with them and work towards enhancing the performance of our staff on the ground. So they were focussed very much on the operational and performance of our monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I just want to be clear on something. Did you say -- the transcript says: "And, I suppose, warfare strategies"?
No, operational strategies, or -- I'm sorry. The CIVPOL operational strategies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. At this stage we'll be examining a number of CIVPOL documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could 65 ter 327 please be shown. Could we zoom in a bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, sir, what is this document about?
It is a memo from myself to Cedric Thornberry, the director of civil affairs. It is dated the 27th of July, 1993, and the subject title is: Crimes committed against Croats in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What period of time does it cover?
Types and numbers of crimes committed against Croats living in Sector South during the period August 1992 to the 31st of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And on the same page, what does it say about the suspects of crimes committed?
It says: "Men in military or police uniforms are suspects for 120 of the 497 crimes committed."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of the document. Now, sir, according to this paragraph, what is the report -- sorry. What is the information contained in this report based on?
Could you enlarge it a little more? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could it please be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, "The attached is a computation of the types and number of crimes reported committed against ethnic Croatians covering the period mid/late August 1992 until the end of May 1993, a period of nine months. This research is based on data which has been taken from UNCIVPOL incident reports. For the purpose of this report, there has been an attempt to categorise this data by type of crime; however, there may be some inaccuracies as there were no standard crime categories used throughout the sectors by all stations. In addition, this data indicates each individual report made, not the number of victims and not necessarily the number of crimes committed. Also, multiple crimes reported on one incident are recorded as one report and categorised under the most serious crime. In updating this data, we have been unable to give a true picture of the situation in the stations that were evacuated after the January the 22nd hostilities. The reason for this is as follows, our monitors have been unable to patrol these areas because of the war situation. Attached is a breakdown of crimes reported by station and backup data."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we scroll further down on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recognise the names on this page?
I do, Your Honour, yes, one is Roberts Noonan and J. Jancewicz, they were both operational officers in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 4 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: A reference is made here to pink zone. What was this? What were these?

The pink zones, Your Honour, were the areas lying between the United Nations protected areas and the confrontation lines. These were areas where, I suppose, the Serbian population would have been the larger proportion of -- or grouping living in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's look now at page 5, the next page, please. If we could enlarge it just a little more. Okay. What does this table represent?

It sets -- it gives a breakdown of the crime incidents or the crime categories, I suppose, would be the correct reference to it, and the reference across the top indicates the station, as referenced on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How many incidents of murder are reported in total, according to this table?
Murder, in total, 29.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What about arson?
Arson, 48.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Assault?
Assault, 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Destruction?
Destruction, 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Intimidation?
Intimidation, 39.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How is destruction defined?
"Destruction is blowing up of buildings with explosives."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what about intimidation?
"Intimidation: Threats through action (firing shots, by throwing stones or other extreme gestures)."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence and assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, may it please be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 726, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let's go back in time a bit. Could 65 ter 330 please be exhibited? Let's zoom in just a little bit. I don't want to lose the entire text on the page, but if we could zoom in a bit more, and let's scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document about?
It is a report from Victor Andreev. He was the head of affairs in Sector South, and it is addressed to Cedric Thornberry, the director of civil affairs. I think it is -- if I could look at the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: If you can scroll up, please?
It is to Cedric Thornberry, director of civil affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now -- please continue.

The report is from Victor Andreev, he is the director of civil affairs at Sector South -- or the head of civil affairs Sector South and it is directed to Cedric Thornberry, the director for civil affairs of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the subject matter is about.

It is -- he is stating that: "I am afraid we have to confirm the facts mentioned in Mr." -- Is it -- I'm not clear of the name there, Your Honour, "letter to me of the 25th of August on situation in Kijevo. I enclose my reply to the Nogolica which gives an account of what we have done to remedy the situation as well as my written report to Martic whom I also intend to see on the matter. "Best regards."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Isn't it written "protest"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My attempt to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Instead of "written report."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, it is "written protest."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you proceed, what is the date? I'm not able to see it clearly at the top. I know the 25th of August is mentioned and which year. Is it possible to zoom in or for the witness to give the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is further -- it is dated the 31st of -- 13th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could the witness indicate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, let's look again at the date, if we could zoom in to that. I see we have zoomed in very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At what, at the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Have we lost the -- there we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, is that the 13th of August, 1992, or the 31st of August, 1992?

The 13 immediately in front of the word "August," but there is also a date on the top which would seem to be a sending date for the message, and that is the 1st of September, 1992. So the probability is that the 31st could be the date of the -- of the document. It's just a -- the structure in dating the document perhaps have the date first, the time then, and the month, but I know at the top you certainly have the date, the 1st of September, 1992, as the date of faxing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, as a matter of practice, can you say anything about the two respective dates, what they would normally refer to? The prior one at the top and then the one that is contained within the box further down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one entered date and time would seem to be the time and the date the document was actually prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I still don't understand. The date that has the date of the 13th of August has just before the number "13" 1815, which is time I suspect. But then also before that 1815 there's "31." I don't know what that means. And the date at the top that refers to the 1st of September, 1992, has 5.16, which could also be time. So when you say the one entered date and time would seem to be the time and the date the document was actually prepared, which one are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one with the time and date -- I know that some monitors used the time -- the date process, where they put the date first, the time next, the month, and the year, and that would seem to be the case there in this date -- time column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one immediately over the box "from V. Andreev," you have 31st, 1815.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But wouldn't you say 5.16 after 1st September 1992 is also a time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would and I would read that as the time the message was sent by fax to some location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the earlier date of August would be the date of preparation of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you know who it was sent -- or it was probably sent to this address, the addressee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to Mr. Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. A document of the 13th is only dispatched on the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I suspect that the date is the 31st because I know some people did use that process for dating, that they put the date first, the time, and then the month and year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, what is this -- what would then be the significance of this "13" before "August"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to assist us, Ms. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, I'll certainly try. Actually, the -- what appears to be a "13" in front of the August is probably actually a "B" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which would mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the letter "B" would refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have appear objection. I don't think the Prosecution can testify about the document. I believe that the witness should be asked about the document and explain as far as he can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can ask the witness another question which would take care of the matter, perhaps. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, the document refers in its body, the content --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And if we could please scroll down. This is the text in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: In that text the date of 25th of August is referred to. Does that suggest that the document was prepared on 31st of August rather than the 13th of August?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are on -- you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we turn to page 3 of this document. And let's scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the name at the bottom of the page?
Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Whose name is it?
It is Victor Andreev.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And once again, he was Victor Andreev?
He was the civil affairs head at Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And now sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's scroll back up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: -- What is this page about?
It is a letter addressed to Mr. Milan Martic, Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: When is it dated?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And let's scroll back up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is dated the 31st of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What is the first paragraph of this letter about?

It says that: "According to our information, there are approximately 50 old Croatian people, mostly women, living under constant fear in Kijevo. They reported that they are constantly harassed and their property stolen by people from the neighbouring village of Polaca. A month ago, two people were murdered and their bodies were found floating in a well. Recently, a drinking water well of one old lady was maliciously contaminated by detergent. These people are terribly afraid and would like to be reassured that their lives and property are protected."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Pardon me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you also read the first three sentences of the second paragraph, the first three sentences will suffice.

"We have actually noticed that the number of cases of harassment, looting, and theft have been increasing recently. In addition to this specific case in Kijevo, we have received disturbing reports from other villages. On Saturday, the 29th of August, in Poljane people dressed in TDF uniforms harassed the villagers and stole their food and money."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What does "TDF" stand for?
They were the Territorial Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: For the Court's information Poljane can be found on page 30 of the precise atlas in grid 2C.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this document be admitted into evidence.
The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit Number 727, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please take a look at 65 ter 337.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we look at that one, the other document -- is this the same document with the date discrepancy? No. There was another one before this one. What do you want to do with that one, the one that has 1st September and 31st --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: It's part of the -- actually, it's the first page of that exhibit and the -- this is the third page that we just spoke of. So it's all part and parcel of Exhibit 65 ter 330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought this was a letter generated by that previous one. Anyway, you know best. Fine. This one has been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: It has been, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we zoom in a bit, please. And let's scroll down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document about?

This, again, is a memo from Victor Andreev, the civil affairs director himself to Mr. Cedric Thornberry. It is, again, dated -- and I think this may clarify the previous one in the sense that where we were looking at 13. It was probably B and this says the letter A. So it would be dated the 27th of October, 1992. So I think that may clarify the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Did you see reports such as these when you worked with UNCIVPOL?
Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, please describe to us or explain, rather, how these reports were generated.

These reports -- the director of civil affairs would make assessment reports and send them to Mr. Thornberry on -- from time to time. And they would, in general, be circulated to us at the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And just to be entirely clear, the term in the subject line: "SITREP"?
Situation report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's turn to page 4 of this document. Please scroll down just a little bit. Thank you. Sir, could you read the first paragraph under the heading "human rights."

"Several areas have remained at the forefront of our preoccupations: Vrljika, Drnis, Korbat, in particular where looting and seizure of Croat properties and food, often with the blessing of the local militia commanders, have increased significantly thereby fanning the of their owners, presently displaced, and their desire to return. We wrote a strong letter of protest to Martic. Our complaints have remained unanswered."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And the next paragraph, there is no need to read it out, just explain what it's about.

Again, indicating that there has been an escalation of crimes over the previous two months. Croatian population have been subjected to violence and intimidation, and again refers to October when five Croats were brutally murdered and homes vacated by Croats have been burned down in a -- probably attempt by Serbs to intimidate the remaining Croats into leaving the Krajina and not allow them to return to -- not to allow the return of displaced persons. "DPs" are referred to as displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: For the Court's information Vrljika can be found on page 31 of the concise atlas in grid C2 and Drnis is on page 30 in grid C2.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, in which sector was Korbat located?
Well, I'm not absolutely sure, but if it's being referred to by Mr. Andreev, I would relate it to being in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And now it's return to the first page of this document. Back to the date and time box, please. What is the date of this document?
It is the 27th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 728, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just note -- actually, my attention has been drawn to it by Judge Hoepfel, that there is now an A what earlier you suggested would be a B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That would clarify the question in exhibit 727. What would that mean, after the hour, to have an E or maybe a B is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Would that be a.m. and p.m. In abbreviated form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But this is clear that this is an A after the hour. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now look at 65 ter 347. Could we zoom in, and let's scroll down a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document about?

It is a report from the information of the UNCIVPOL liaison officer Belgrade sector -- again, from Sector South. It's a daily situation report. It is dated the 22nd of February, 1993, and it is addressed to the UNCIVPOL headquarters at Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's --
And it's -- it's from the UNCIVPOL headquarters in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's scroll down on this page, please. And let's look at the last few sentences on page 1 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, could you read aloud the part which commences: "It has also been reported"?

"It has also been reported earlier that about 100 Croats have left their homes in the Medvidja area and are living in the caves, fields, and forests for fear of being murdered or robbed by the local turned bandits soldiers. The CIVPOL monitors also received confirmed information from the Benkovac milicija chief Slobodan Vujko, that for the past week between 11 and 17 Croats have been murdered and one woman raped."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: For the Court's information, Medvidja is located on page 25 in grid D2 of the concise atlas. Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit Number 729, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Ms. Valabhji, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: The word "milicija" is referred to this document and we will see it later as well. What does this term refer to?
It refers to the police in -- it would refer to the RSK police within the mission area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And while we're on this topic, let's take a look at 65 ter 343. Sir, what is this document about?

It is an organisational chart showing the -- I suppose the structure future man-power level of the milicija, and I understand it is from the -- refers to Sector North, milicija in Sector North, and it is dated the 29th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what does MIL info sect refer to?
I think it refers to the military information section, it's talking about Sector North, so it would be addressed to the military element or component of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And let's scroll further down this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we scroll down, is my memory failing me? I thought when you explained the various sectors of UNPROFOR, Knin was Sector South.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this is Sector North and I see Knin is written here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If my memory is correct, there is a footnote at the end to indicate it refers to -- the information may have come to light in a meeting with Sector North.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, according it this document how were the milicija to be organised?

This document shows that "7.000 regular milicija responsible for normal law and order and other milicija-performed functions. This milicija is to be dressed in regular milicija uniforms and armed with side-arms and batons. And then there were 16.000 special milicija or purpose milicija organised in eight BDEs," I'm not sure what that means, "each consisting of about 2.000 men. "The special purpose milicija is divided into special milicija and border milicija of which the latter is by far the largest contributor concerning number of men. "This milicija would be responsible for policing the borders and protect population from threat of terrorist attacks. "This milicija to be armed with long rifles."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 730, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, this document that we just looked at refers to the special-purpose milicija. How was the special-purpose milicija regarded by UN monitors?

The -- it seems at a very early stage that there were two types of police on the mission. One was what we regarded as a professional -- as professional police officers. It was apparent that they were that, and I suspect that they were part of the original police force in existence prior to the break-up. And then there was another group, to be quite frank, they did not possess any principles of policing. They were certainly regarded as the problem on the mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which of these two would you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 2.000 group I would -- or the 7.000 group, within that, we regarded them as professional police officers. Certainly a lot of people came to prominence there that we considered professional police officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the 16.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would regard them and indeed they were held in general regard by all the monitors by not conforming to any of the principles of policing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And how did you know this?

It came to our notice through a variety of sources, I suppose, firstly, our own monitors on the ground dealing with them. The local community made numerous reports of incidents where they were involved, and indeed they were absolutely terrorised of them. Professional police officers within their own grouping, that would be the 7.000 grouping, had indicated to us that there were people operating in a manner that they do not condone. They also expressed views and concerns, and indeed that is documented, that they had particular difficulties in dealing with certain situations when these people were involved. In other words, these people seemed to be -- unaccountability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you are thinking, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take the break. We will come back at quarter to 11.00. Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, before the break we were talking about the special-purpose milicija or police. Did you know who was in command of the special-purpose police?
Yes, Your Honour, it is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Who was that?
Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And how did you know this?

I knew it from contacts with the police in the various sectors and, indeed, particularly Sector South, and it was common knowledge within our headquarters as well, to civil affairs, the military element. It was common knowledge that he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: While we're on the same topic, that is the term "milicija," let's take a look at 65 ter 333. Let's zoom in. That's perfect. Sir, what is this document?
It is a status report dated the 7th of September, 1992, and Sector South is referred to. And it's on the Serbo-Croatian conflict and UNPROFOR mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Were you given an opportunity to review it earlier this week?
Yes, Your Honour, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's scroll down this page. And let's turn to the next page, which is page 2 of the document. Please scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the contents of this document?

I do not recall it -- once I saw it initially, I did not recall it there and then, but I can say that everything that came through our office I did read. And again, the assessment would have been reasonably familiar to me, but when I saw it at the time I cannot say there and then yes I remember that. But looking at the contents it would be familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: When you say "looking at the contents it would be familiar," what do you mean, can you elaborate?
In other words the assessment is something I would have become aware of and, I suppose, would have knowledge of as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What was that -- what is that assessment?
It is referred to here. Do you wish me to read?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes. Please read the first paragraph under this heading "power struggle in 'RSK'"?

"Martic is in charge, but he is not a gang chief -- he is a gang chief, not a political leader. He appears as an executor of plans commenced out of Knin -- conceived out of Knin." Perhaps you can enlarge a little bit, my sight is variable. Is that possible? Okay. I just wish to stay in front of the mike as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sure.

"Reshaping of power structure ongoing consists of Martic's band (Ducic) getting rid of the moderates, through terror. Four ... Moderates have been fired recently, four and -- so-called moderates, yeah, have been fired recently. "Spanovic is compelled to get close to him under threat. He looks increasingly hard-liner. They need one another. No decision-makers and not even valid interlocutors for us in Knin. "Although the new balance of power is not clear yet and though internal dispute is predominant, Militia is in power throughout the 'Krajina,' more than civil authorities. Milicijas are not in private army but the translation on the ground of the 'new shaped Krajina state in progress.' They show devotion to him, imposing his kind of new 'militia order' and rules through force. His group is expanding ethnic cleansing systematically. Also in Krajina. "Martic never gave to us indications to adhere to the Vance Plan. On the contrary, he has repeatedly stated in public that he will -- that there will be no restoration of Croatian authority and that the cease-fire line is the border of the 'RSK' state."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: In the previous paragraph the word "his" is used, "his group," "his private army." Who's being referred to here?
The militia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Actually, maybe I should clarify. The word "his," which person might be referred to in this paragraph by that possessive pronoun?
It's -- Mr. Martic is the person referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn now to page 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be grateful at this stage for the purpose of the last question on this document if I could distribute hard copies, as I'll be asking the witness to compare the fifth and sixth pages of the document to the first two pages, and hard copies may facilitate this exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Martic is not -- does not have the translation on his screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can somebody help Mr. Martic to get the translation on his screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could I have the assistance of the usher in distributing a hard copy of the B/C/S translation to the accused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, could you take a look at page 5 of the document and compare it to the first page. Are there differences? Are they the same? Could you explain.

Yes, I was shown both documents, and I suppose I have -- I cannot explain entirely why the second one is there, but on reading it I did notice some -- different words along the way, and the view I came to was that the -- what is referred to in the second document, that is 426074, could be a draft. Some words were refined, and it's on that basis I would go towards suggesting it is a draft.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has an objection to the tendering of the documents because all the past documents which had to be with UNCIVPOL, there was a cover page or at least a reference to the effect that this was a document produced by the organisation, date, author of the document, who it was addressed to, who received it, when it was sent. There was even a reference to the effect as to whether this took place in the morning or in the afternoon, whether it was sent as a telegram. And none of the references I mentioned are contained here, and the witness merely read parts of it out. And I don't think that this document can, in fact, be admitted as an UNCIVPOL document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all I would direct my learned colleague to the Trial Chamber's guidelines issued on the admissibility of documents, and these guidelines explicitly state that the practice will be in favour of admissibility. Moreover, it states that the fact that a document isn't signed or isn't stamped it does not render it a priori void of authenticity. On this basis alone the document is admissible. In addition, it is not the case that the witness merely read out paragraphs from that document. If I could refer to the transcript, the witness also mentioned that, in other words, the assessment in the document is something that he would have become aware of and that he supposed he would have knowledge of as well. This is at lines 8 and 9. I think the document is admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the instruction my learned friend referred to, the guidelines have in mind a document which may be a copy of the original not bearing any signatures because it was produced in several copies; however, here we have nothing, no heading. The fact that the document is in the context of the witness's testimony does not automatically mean that this is an UNCIVPOL document -- besides the formulations used in the document are far from diplomatic. And the question is, who signed the document or, perhaps, refused to sign it. The witness has also explained not remembering having read the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you direct the Chamber, Mr. Milovancevic, to the portion of the guidelines which contemplates a copy and not an original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not my intention to refer you to the guidelines. I was commenting on the interpretation of the guidelines put forth by my learned friend. I said that in addition to the guidelines, which are quite clear, reasonable, and have to be adhered to, we, at any rate, can assess whether something is a document or not. Our position as Defence is that one cannot make out who the author of this particular text is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, shall I quote what you said and then you can tell me what you meant. Page 42, line 5, 10:59:38, you say: "The guidelines have in mine a document which may be a copy of the original not bearing any signatures because it was produced in several copies ..." Now I'm asking you to direct the Chamber in the guidelines to that portion which says that the document must be a copy for it to be admitted without a signature. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I said this - and you have accurately repeated it - it was not my intention to quote the guidelines. I was responding to my learned friend's submissions and interpreting the guidelines, and I was providing you with my interpretation of them. I was trying to apply the guidelines to this specific instance. This was, therefore, not quoting the guidelines, but merely giving you my interpretation of them where I wanted to say that the document is practically impossible to identify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you then please direct the Chamber to that portion of the guideline which gives you the basis for the interpretation that you have just given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with me for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in mind paragraphs 5 and 6 of the guidelines governing these matters, where paragraph 5 deals with a document which is not signed and does not bear any stamps and with the status that may be accorded to such a document, whereas paragraph 6 goes on to deal with the admissibility and non-admissibility of documents and how the parties are to proceed on these matters. Paragraph 6 even provides for the possibility for the party referring to the document to check the authenticity of documents presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not my wish to claim that the absence of a signature or a stamp automatically shows inadmissibility of a document; I wanted to say that we could not identify this document as an UNCIVPOL document. The fact -- or rather, had the witness recognised the document as the document produced by himself or the team he worked with, then we would not call this matter into question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Milovancevic, two things I would have liked you to do for me. I would have liked you to have quoted me paragraphs 5 and 6, but starting with the very last point you are making, my understanding of the witness is that he did not immediately recognise but that when he looked at it was a document that would have been generated in his office. And he thus said that in fact the page 5 is a draft of page 1. That's how he explains it. That's how he recognised it. I don't know whether you are suggesting that the witness should be able to recognise each and every document that was generated by his office at first glance. Is that what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I clarify something, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just hold it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I'm not suggesting that, Your Honour. What you have said is beyond doubt that the witness has recognised the topic the document deals with, and it is a fact that the witness stated that this is likely to be a document that was generated in his office. However, there are no other elements for any further inferences on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In your initial objection one of the elements that you said was lacking from this document was the date, and it does have a date. And I can remember this Chamber admitting documents which were not even generated by the witness or by the witness's office. You will remember that there was a witness who came here and referred to newspaper cuttings and had to confirm that the -- what was mentioned in the newspaper cuttings was what he had seen. Now, that newspaper cutting was not generated by him. That's one point. The next point, you say that -- in your objection, for the document to be admitted, it must show who it was addressed to. Now, not all documents are addressed to anybody, they may be records. And who received it and when it was sent. Now, all those points you are raising are not, to my knowledge, points that go to admissibility of the document. Now, I'm reading here at page 5 [sic], lines 2 to 12, which is your initial objection. If you have -- do you still have anything to say, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all the arguments that you have put forward are absolutely in keeping with what has been done so far. In other words, these are the elements that have always governed the Trial Chamber to admit a document or not. In this particular document, our concern is the fact that this document is absolutely different from any other that has been presented so far. Even on its page 2, in its left upper corner, it says this was compiled by the sector or the staff or something to that effect and it is being sent to whoever, and it also bears a number, whereas this document does not have any of that on any of the pages. I'm absolutely clear that one page may be missing some of the elements that might identify either the author or the document itself. And our concern is that those elements are missing from all the pages. The fact that this document is different from the first one may be interpreted by the fact that it is a draft, but this is the witness's conclusion. He concludes that this might be a draft, although the document itself doesn't show anything to point to the fact that it might be a draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done? The Chamber is going to give its ruling. The document is going to be admitted into evidence. Obviously the weight that is going to be attached to the document is something that will be dealt with at the time of assessing the evidence. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be the Exhibit Number 731, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, we've just looked at several reports from Sector South in 1992 and 1993 and discussed various aspects of them. What do these aspects of the reports show, in your view?

The overall reports, to me, indicated that the Croatian population was the subject of extreme violence, harassment, and the level of that violence is absolutely extreme. In some of the documents there is reference to entire families being wiped out, killed. It was clear as well that the militia played an active part in a lot of the incidents. There were men in uniform mentioned on many occasions. On specific occasions militia were mentioned. Also, specific militia men were mentioned. And I think they also indicated that the militia failed to take any positive action to deal with the issues. I think that the objective was to terrorise the people and, effectively, have them leave the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: The next set of documents are, for the most part, reports and they will be discussed in chronological order. Let's take a look at 65 ter 324.

That is a report dated the 29th of May, 1992, from the CIVPOL sector chief in Sector South. And it is addressed to the force commander, General Sameer. Again, this is a situation report for Sector South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. McElligott, Mr. Milovancevic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for the interruption. Mr. Martic is not receiving -- has not received the B/C/S versions of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, could we help Mr. Martic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: May I have the assistance of the usher, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to page 2 of this document. Could we scroll down to the bottom of the page, please. Further down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the signature on this page?
Yes, I do, and the name, Sameer, Bino, yes, I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And who was Sameer, Bino.
He was the sector chief in Sector South for a period, and he was subsequently attached to headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's scroll further up this page. Further up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What does the heading under "expulsion of Croats" mean?

It says: "Every effort has been made by CIVPOL to ensure their safety within the UNPA Sector South. All reports to CIVPOL offices are investigated to a satisfactory conclusion allowing order to be restored and confidence in UNPROFOR. Despite these efforts by CIVPOL to ensure their safety the local milicija are continuing to undermine and intimidate these people. The local community are frightened to disclose information to UNPROFOR because the likelihood of retaliation from the local milicija."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. Could it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 732, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look at 65 ter number 328, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document about?
This is a report from superintendent McGowan to Mr. Thornberry. It's dated the 20th of August, 1992, and the subject is robbery and larceny from elderly Croatian people in Vrljika area of pink zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature at the top?
Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?
It is that of P. J. McGowan.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And who was P. J. McGowan?
He was head of operations at the CIVPOL headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page three of this document. Could we scroll -- rather, zoom in to the -- well, first to the top bit. Yeah. Thank you. Briefly, what is this page about?
