It refers to criminal acts, and specifically refers to Wednesday, the 12th of August, 1992, made contact with citizen in the area of Maovice near Vrljika. I accompanied by PC and CIVPOL interpreter. "The citizen's name is Ive Rezic - elderly man. "He complained about a robbery committed by uniformed milicija men. "He informed CIVPOL that on Sunday, the 9th of August, 1992, 10.00 two uniformed policemen arrived at his home. He described one of the men as follows: "Man, about 32-years-old, height 1.80 kilometres, dark skin. "He was wearing uniform with Serbian Krajina on the sleeve. He named him at Jurca Graovac from Stinovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's scroll further down the page.

"No description of the other man. "They were driving in a red car. "Reg. number not known. "Using violence, the two men threatened the old man to give them all his food. "They stole: 50 kilogrammes of sugar and 2 kilogrammes of bacon. "The two men hit the old man, they knocked him to the ground and bumped his head against the floor. We did not see any visible signs of violence in the old man's face, but he seemed to be very frightened."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: You can complete what you were saying?
"He was reluctant first to report the matter to the local police."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, could it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 733, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I have a question concerning these handwritten markings on the first they; they have appeared also on other documents. Can you, Mr. McElligott, maybe explain to us what this note means on the left top corner of the first page? Can we go to the first page again? And here it says: "File" -- it 403521.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has no significant meaning to me, Your Honour, neither have the other ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The other thing is on the right-hand top corner it says: "1.2.4." Does that have any meaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not. No, I don't recall it having any specific meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Similar markings appeared also on this which we discussed earlier, Exhibit 731. Thank you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, keeping in mind the document we've just viewed, could 65 ter 329 please be shown. Now, let's turn to page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, from whom is this document?
It is Mr. Cedric Thornberry, director of civil affairs at UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And let's return to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: To whom is it addressed?
It is addressed to Mr. Prjec. I understand him to be the head of the militia or commissioner of militia in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: When is this document dated?
It is dated the 24th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what's it's about?
It is a letter of complaint to Mr. Prjec in relation to two incidents, and it is a demand, as supposed to rectify some standards in relation to his policing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's return to page 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we return to page 2. Can I just ask -- you've told us what UNPROFOR stands for, or what is -- oh, I beg your pardon, it's okay. Sorry. You can go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could just look briefly again at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you read the line on this page.
"I ask that you use your good influence to examine these cases and see that justice is not only done but seen to be done."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit Number 734, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look at 65 ter number 336.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Circumstances what is this document about?

It is a document addressed to the UNCIVPOL headquarters in Zagreb from the HG UNCIVPOL at Sector South. And it is signed by the Sector chief K. G. Andersson, yes, addressed to the chief of operations, which is probably myself. It is dated the 2nd of October, 1994, and it's -- the subject is: "The destruction of a church."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I wonder, could that be 1992?
It is 1992, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's look further down the document. What is it about?

It's re: Your message of the 2nd of October, 1992. "St. Ann's church is or was located in Zvjerinac, which is a part of the village Kosovo, south of Knin. (Mentioned in SITREP 1/10/92.) "By mistake the CIVPOL has written the wrong grid reference on the initial report, and the correct grid should be 978-689. "Please find attached requested report."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And where was the church located?
The church is -- St. Ann's church is located in -- I'll spell it. It is Z-v-j-e-r-i-n-a-c, which is a part of the village Kosovo, K-o-s-o-v-o, south of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Any idea what religious denomination the church belonged to?
St. Ann's, I would regard it as a Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of the document. Let's scroll down. When did this incident occur?

At 7.30 a.m. On the 1st of October, CIVPOL station Knin received a telephone call from unknown name, from Kosovo. These persons said that St. Ana church was destroyed. We informed the milicija at 8.00 and we went to Bvac hamlet of Kosovo where is situated the church. At 9.00 a.m. When we arrived we saw Santa Anna church fully destroyed."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence and assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. Could it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit Number 735, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could exhibit number 65 ter 338 please be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document?

It is a briefing monthly report, dated the 2nd of November, 1992, UNPROFOR civilian police Sector South, and it is a briefing about UNCIVPOL Sector South on the visit of the 4th Commander, the director of civil affairs and the deputy force commander -- Colonel Campose.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Is the format of the document familiar to you?
Yes, indeed it is, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of this document. And please scroll down the page. Let's enlarge the text in zone -- pertaining to zone B. That's great.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what does it say in the paragraph pertaining to Knin?

"Knin: Many incidents of theft has been reported from the village of Kijevo. On the 1st of October, the church Santa Ana in Kosovo was destroyed. During the month of October some incidents have been reported from Kninskopolje, K-n-i-n-s-k-o-p-o-l-j-e, where Croatian people have been threatened and someone shot on their houses. Some people now want to leave for the Croatian side. "A lot of thefts from UNCIVPOL have been reported in Knin." That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Please look at the very last paragraph on page 2. What does it say about the milicija?
Whereabouts -- oh, yes, at the very end. "However, UNCIVPOL have good cooperation with the Milicija in Vrljika."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you comment on this, please.

On occasions there was good levels of cooperation. It tended to be switched on and switched off on certain occasions. We did have situations where there was a constant flow of good contact. And I suppose if I wanted to single out a particular area I would look at Korenica, and I think that there was a steady, consistent, positive approach, I would describe, in that area of keeping things pretty good. I think if we looked at the report this morning where we had a reference to each station and the crimes committed in it, it may also reflect that trend so that, you know -- there was an absolute frustrating level of blocking done put -- there were points along the way where good things did happen and very often those good things were done to individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for that clarification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say on occasions there was good levels of cooperation and it tends to be switched on and switched off on certain occasions, cooperation from who between the two milicijas, the 7.000 or the 16.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 7.000 were the corner-stone to making progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And here at Vrljika, which one are you referring to, which -- which milicija are you referring to, the 7.000 or the 16.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I would suspect that it boils down to individual contacts. Perhaps there was an individual or a couple of individuals in that area at a given time, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- there was a relationship built up between them and our monitors and progress was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But when you say: On occasions there was good levels of cooperation, that was the comment you were making on the Vrljika police station --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- Milicija. My question is: Which of these two milicija are you referring to vis-a-vis Vrljika when you say there was good cooperation? Was it the 7.000 or the 16.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cooperation came from the 7.000 group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's look at page 3 of this document, in prisoner of war under the heading "Benkovac." Please scroll down. Now, what information is provided in the first and fourth paragraphs under Benkovac?

"Benkovac: Two persons were killed on the 2nd of the 10th in the village of Dobro Polje, D-o-b-r-o P-o-l-j-e. The living conditions for people in many villages in Benkovac are very bad, i.e., Bijeljina, where about 25 Croatians have to stay out in the fields during the night, because they are afraid to be killed."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And the fourth paragraph?
The fourth paragraph: "And many of the Croatian citizens have applied to leave the UNPAs, and during one month UNCIVPOL received 155 such applications."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could this document please be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 736, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look at 65 ter 339. Could we make it a little bit bigger. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document about?
It is a daily situation report prepared at UNCIVPOL headquarters, and it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now -- please continue.
It is dated the 8th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of the document, and let's enlarge it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What is the date on this document -- on this page, rather?
The date is the 8th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's now turn to page 4, and please scroll to the second half of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What information is provided in the first paragraph under Roman numeral V?

V: "Kostajnica CIVPOL received the complaint from Croats living in the village of Timarci where they are threatened every night by Serbs wearing masks. They also stated that their church was blown up on the 22nd of -- or at 2230 hours last night. They were afraid of complaining to the local police that CIVPOL informed and will monitor about this case. "CIVPOL also noted two destroyed houses in Kukuruzari, K-u-k-u-r-u-z-a-r-i. They were not occupied since the owner named Juric left the area before the war."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And let's scroll up, further up the page, to the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Which sector is being referred to?
Again, Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look at 65 ter 340, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What is this document about?
It's -- perhaps you could enlarge --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- it's a daily situation report, and the general -- yeah -- dated the 10th of November, 1992 -- or it has a reference date on the 11th of November, 1992, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you summarise what the first paragraph on this page indicates. It's the paragraph starting: "The operational situation ..."

It refers to the operational situation in Sector South. And it says: "The operational situation in Sector South is in a very difficult situation due to the increasing number of incidents and the low percentage of incidents which is cleared up by the local police. Monitors are getting a -- very little response from the local police and the situation is tense in the whole sector. Many people of Croatian origin wish to leave the UNPA because they are not feeling safe. Monitors are feeling that they cannot help this person -- persons but will although try to do their best."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 738, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I only have a few more documents. Let's take a look at 65 ter 342, please, and let's enlarge it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to see it?
Perhaps you could go further.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay.
Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document about?
It is a document dated the 25th of December, 1992. It's from UNCIVPOL headquarters Sector South to the HG at Zagreb. And again, it is a daily situation report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of the document. And could we enlarge the top part. Sir, could you read aloud the part which commences: "They also discussed ..." It's about halfway down the top text at the top.

"They also discussed a new 'so-called customs' rules now being enforced by the milicija at crossing points, where food items, electronic items, and even cash is being confiscated. It was discussed to the failure of the milicija to report serious crimes immediately to CIVPOL stations, without delay. Current investigations by Knin station."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is Exhibit Number 739.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we now please look at 65 ter 344, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document about?

It is a document from the UNCIVPOL HQ at Sector South from K. G. Andersson, the sector chief, addressed to the CIVPOL headquarters at Zagreb. It is dated the 31st of April -- or of February 1993, and it's -- its subject: Your message of the 2nd of the 2nd, 1993, murder reports, and it is actually addressed to me, for my attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's just --
Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like some water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the date and time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Zoom in on the?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Date and time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the 31st of February, 1993, are the 3rd -- sorry, the 3rd of February, 1993, at 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again. It's not the 31st, it's the 3rd, the 3rd of February, at 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's turn to page 3, and let's look at the last paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: In brief, what is this paragraph about?

It has reference to a dead Croatian women at Kijevo with grid reference provided. "The body of this woman was found in a field near this village, near the roadside. The skin on the head had almost completely been removed. The skull had a large hole in it on the left side indicating a blunt object like a stone may have been used. These observations were made by a CIVPOL monitor. Milicija was contacted and attended but refused to investigate or look after the body. CIVPOL took the body to Knin hospital where they refused to do an autopsy and demanded UNPROFOR take the body away and look after the burial. CIVPOL left the body there, insisting that it was the" --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "It was the responsibility of the local authorities. There has been a total lack of cooperation with CIVPOL in this case."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And the next paragraph, could you tell us what that indicates.

"This area, which is in the Vrljika CIVPOL station area is inhabited by only older Croatian people, mostly old women. Over the past months they have been systematically robbed, beaten, harassed, terrorised, and now murdered, almost on a daily basis. Local authorities have not been able to stop it. The suspects as reported by CIVPOL Vrljika were actual members of the milicija or border milicija. Some suspects in these crimes were actually under investigation by milicija and the investigative court over the past months; however, the cases were never completed."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. Membership be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 740, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the last document for today, 65 ter 348, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, what is this document about, sir?

It is a document dated the 20th of April, 1993, from Cedric Thornberry to Jim Baldie, who was the CS -- the director of the, I suppose -- he was the director of administrative affairs in the mission. And again the subject is: "Protection of minorities in Sector North. "Attached is self-explanatory correspondence. It would be very much appreciated if the logistical equipment necessary to carry out this most urgent and vital humanitarian task could be provided as soon as possible." And that is signed by Cedric Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I was just about to recognise you, do you recognise the signature?
I do indeed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of the document. Could we enlarge it slightly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This, again, is a note from the CIVPOL commissioner Michael O'Rielly and again the subject is: "Intimidation and board of human" -- which I suppose board of human rights in villages near Glina, Sector North. "A report from the chief Sector North shows that crimes against minorities (Croats) have increased to such an unacceptable level that the residents of the villages (all elderly people) are living out in the woods at night. The sector chief has forwarded a comprehensive proposal with new initiatives -- initiative to tackle this problem and add to the quality of life of those affected. Speedy logistical support is essential to ensure immediate action. Support from your office is requested."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think it says invitations.
Invitations, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit Number 741, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you now about visits to sectors in the course of your work with UNCIVPOL. Did you visit sectors when you worked with UNCIVPOL?

Yes, Your Honour. After taking up my initial appointment, I just familiarised myself at HQ for some days, and then I travelled -- spent a two-week period travelling to every station in the mission area, where I went out and viewed every situation first-hand. Subsequent to that, I would have made a number of visits to the sectors, specifically to meet up with monitors to assess how they were managing their affairs and giving them any support and encouragement we could. We also had meetings with the administrative staff at the district headquarters where we met staff to evaluate and support them in the work right down to ground level. I visited again on numerous occasions to follow-up on specific events and on each occasion would go to station level, travel with monitors on patrols, and see first-hand what was actually happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you meet with Croat civilians from the sectors?

I did, yes, I met with a number of them. I met them at places where they resided out in the countryside, even in the CIVPOL stations when -- where they called, and I availed them of opportunity to speak with them on their circumstances. And I suppose the one strong memory I have is that they were absolutely terrorised, they were totally insecure, they were -- some of them recounted sleeping out in the forest. I remember one lady describing sleeping in the forest with her young daughter at night in the middle of winter, and I suppose it was a horrific thing to listen to. It was hard to credit that people could be treated with such insensitivity. They just did not-- not know -- they didn't know what to do with themselves. They didn't know whether to stay and put up with the horror they were doing or to leave and go into an unknown world. So it was an incredible scenario.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall which sectors these visits pertained to?
Generally Sectors South and North were the areas where those situations really arose.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony you mentioned that you worked with UNPROFOR, based in Zagreb, from October 1992 until November 1993 -- pardon me. Let's clarify that, actually. Could you tell us again from when to when did you work with UNPROFOR.
From the 2nd of October, 1992, to the 1st of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During the course of your work, how many situation reports did you review, approximately?

I would have reviewed every situation report prepared in the mission during my stay there, and certainly a substantial amount of them prepared in advance of my arrival to read my way into the situation. So I would say I have read every situation report prepared up to the date I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: About how many, would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was there 13 months, so one was prepared every day of the week, so we're talking about perhaps I would have reviewed overall perhaps 400 or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What did these reports indicate to you? What general impressions did you form?

They gave a profile of the mission on a daily basis, and I suppose they set out what was happening on the ground. They -- what I suppose they marked out was that the minority population of Croatians were subjected to extremely -- extreme violence. They were murdered, they were intimidated, their communities were attacked in the sense of houses were burnt in groups, churches were destroyed, which effectively deprived them of a place -- to gather and pray, and indeed, I suppose to gather as a community. So it was literally breaking down the community. The perpetrators, I suppose, there are clear indications that the police component within the mission was responsible for a lot of these things. They certainly did little to prevent any of them, and there was no accountability. Now, having said that, we did meet some fine police officers, too, and I want to reflect that as well. There were policemen we met on the mission who were on the Serbian side, and they were honourable, professional police officers. They declared that publicly to us, and indeed I had conversations with some them myself. And they did indicate to me privately that they did not condone what was happening. So I think it's important to mark that, too. But there was a group who do not do credit to anybody. I suppose it was hard to believe that anybody could treat elderly people with such disrespect. Most of the victims who have been profiled in the reports show that they are very old people. Many of the dates of births go back to 1920 to 1940, so effectively we had people terrorising their grandparents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Are there any particular incidents of crimes that you became aware of that are particularly etched in your memory?

Yes, indeed. I suppose when you profile what has happened, it would be hard to say something stands beyond them all, but there were two. And one was an incident where somebody was killed and they were scalped, and another incident a very old lady was found nailed to the floor of her home. So I think when you reflect on those it describes it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What were the nationality of the victims in these two cases?
They were Croats, Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And in what sectors were these incidentals?
Sectors North and south.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for coming to testify?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Valabhji. Mr. -- I don't know, Mr. Milovancevic, whether you want to start. We are two or three minutes to adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has a request to make of the Trial Chamber. Mr. Martic -- or rather, his Defence team has yesterday, today, and several days ago received translations of the documents which are all in English. Mr. Martic is kindly requesting for some time to become acquainted with the material. The documents were really received by him at the last moment, at the 11th hour, and he did not have time to familiarise himself with the documents and we kindly ask to start our cross-examination on Monday rather than today. And we would like to make use of the time with a view to being fully prepared for our cross-examination on Monday. At any rate, this would not be time lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Valabhji, would have anything to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have a moment to confer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that additional time is required for the following reasons. Certainly not until -- delay until Monday. First of all, the substance of the testimony of this witness was disclosed months ago, earlier this year; and second, the substance or, rather, the information contained in these exhibits could have been explained by counsel, who I understand speak English, to their client. And second -- and third, finally, I don't believe that the Rules provide for or, rather, require the translation into B/C/S of English documents. I don't think there is this requirement in the Rules. This is done as a courtesy, and this is our position, Your Honour. Your Honour, may I just add one more thing. I haven't been able to verify exactly when all the translations were disclosed this week. I think counsel mentioned yesterday, today, and several days ago -- pardon me, I misunderstood. I think that's fine. I withdraw this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to find, either in the Statute or in the Rules -- I seem to recollect that there is a requirement that the accused shall be tried in a language he understands -- or put it this way. If he doesn't understand there shall be interpretation for him and documents shall be given to him in the language that he understands. Can somebody help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's the Appeals Chamber decision listing precisely the documents to be translated. We can find this over the break and present to the Trial Chamber. At any rate, both the provisions of the Statute and the Rules in their substance, and in addition to that the practice in this case has been such that the accused has to have documents against him in his own language to be able to respond. The fact that several thousand documents were, in fact, delivered and disclosed several years ago does not give the entitlement to the Prosecution not to deliver the accused the documents that are precisely related to his case because these documents go to Mr. Martic's activities and the activities of his police. Without having the appropriate translations, we were unable to prepare ourselves fully for the proceedings, because in this case the OTP has departed from the practice and the obligations that both sides have had to meet in this case so far. This is the decision in the case in Ljubicic dated November 2002, 2nd November --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision lists the documents that have to be delivered to the accused in a language he understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand what you say, Mr. Milovancevic, but I was also trying to find support from either the Rules or the Statute, quite apart from the fact, Ms. Valabhji, that the practice since we started this trial has been to try and provide -- to provide translations whenever -- whenever the Defence has given documents, we have asked them to give us translations as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I should confer since I'm not -- I would like to confer with co-counsel on this matter some more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest that now that we're virtually in the break time, we adjourn for the break and you confer during the break. Court adjourned, come back at half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we find it difficult to believe that the Defence is not in a position to commence its cross-examination today for the following reasons. First of all, I've obtained the information that the first of these translations that amounts to three translations the first is disclosed on the 17th of May, 2006, and today, I believe, is the 26th. That was nine days ago. Surely the Defence is in a position to cross-examine if they have questions to ask about these today. Second, as mentioned earlier, the substance of the testimony of this witness was discussed a long time ago, earlier this year, and the B/C/S translation of his statement was also disclosed earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The B/C/S translation of the witness's statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Of the witness's statement informing of the areas that the witness would testify about. Finally, again what I mentioned earlier is that the substance of the information contained in these exhibits can be explained to Mr. Martic, the accused, by his counsel. So there is no -- it's not the case that the accused is completely deprived of the opportunity to find out what's in these documents. In fact, a list informing the Defence of the documents to be used with this witness was sent several days ago. This was last Friday. And a follow-up e-mail indicated the final list earlier this week. Now, the other point I'd like to mention is that in this case we have had exhibits admitted that are in English. These were exhibits 204 and 205, and they were admitted on the 17th of February, 2006. Finally, Your Honours, I have the Trial Chamber decision in the Ljubicic case of the 20th of November, 2002. The Defence quoted -- or rather, referred to an Appeals Chamber decision, but that is actually not the case. It's a decision at the first instance of 20th November 2002. And the decision on page 3, and I have hard copies, should that assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It certainly will assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: May I direct Your Honours to page 3 of the decision. In the middle of the page in a noting paragraph, it says that: "During the trial stage the incumbent Chamber may direct the Prosecutor to tender exhibits or the relevant parts of such exhibits either in hard copy or in audio format in a language understood by the accused." The operative word is "may direct the Prosecutor," and on this basis, Your Honour, I think that some of the submissions made earlier in relation to this decision may not be entirely in line with the text of the decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you sit down, Ms. Valabhji, you said that a list of the documents -- of the exhibits that was going to be used -- that were going to be used in this case or by this witness was submitted to the Defence when? Last week, on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: It was on Friday last week, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you is: Were the exhibits themselves not delivered to the Defence? You said a list of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: These exhibits have been previously disclosed to the Defence, Your Honour. Now, I have to verify this, the exact date of their disclosure, but by and large these were 65 ter exhibits, that is exhibits filed with the Prosecution's exhibit list, and that exhibit list was filed on the 7th of May, 2004. So therefore these documents - and it's easy to verify this - but I'm pretty sure that these documents were all disclosed in 2004 in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am surprised, Your Honours, that my learned friend says that the accused has not been completely deprived from familiarising himself with the material that he has been -- completely been deprived. He has the right to completely familiarise himself with the material. Here we are departing from the practice that has been present in the case so far. I'm wondering how come so much money has been spent by this Tribunal for the translation of the materials so far, and this is not being done in this case. Mr. Martic could simply not study the documents that were delivered. It would be very professional if my learned friend said: This is an omission on my part, and we apologise. I wonder what this means. Why is my learned friend insisting on this? This is not about me or Mr. Perovic, my co-counsel, being able to cross-examine; it is about the right of the accused to know what we are cross-examining about, and the witness has travelled from afar to be examined and cross-examined. And the accused has the right to know what the cross-examination is about. I think we're wasting time here. This discussion is futile. The -- in simple terms, the essential right of the accused has been impaired here. I'm not saying that this has been done deliberately, and I'm sure that it is a result of a string of circumstances, but if we are going to start talking about the rights of the accused, then the right of the accused to understand and to follow things that concern him should not be jeopardised in any way and should never come into question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you're standing up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, if there is some kind of comment on professionalism, I take objection to that. What I have said, and it's reflected in the transcript, is that we are surprised that they are not in a position to start today, and then I set out the reasons why that was, including the delivery of translations of at least three documents on the 17th of May, 2006, which is about nine days ago. In addition to that, I mentioned the ability of counsel to explain the substance of what's in the exhibits to their client, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have to rehash your argument. I understand your objection. What I did want to ask you, Mr. Milovancevic, is whether -- or even before I ask you, Mr. Milovancevic, let me ask you, Ms. Valabhji. You're talking of three documents that were delivered on the 17th. I think we have tendered more than three documents through this witness. What about the other documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The other documents, I'm informed that the disclosures took place on the 22nd, the 23rd, the 24th of May, 2006. So therefore, the last disclosures took place on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sorry, this is the B/C/S translations of the English documents. Now, the original English, of course, were disclosed a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the Chamber is going to take a robust approach to this problem, and it's going to be based on just the fairness to the accused. If B/C/S translations have been delivered to the Defence as recently as the 24th and 22nd of May this year, I think it's in all fairness that the accused be given an opportunity to look at those documents and give his counsel proper instructions. I understand that this may be -- this may not necessarily be in terms of the Rules, but you have referred me to the Ljubicic judgement where you said the court "may." In this case the Defence is not asking that they be given B/C/S translations; they are just asking for time to study the material and be able to take instructions from their client. I think that's a reasonable request. Their request is, therefore, granted. That being the case, you will be in a position to start with your cross-examination on Monday, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Later this afternoon I'm going to visit Mr. Martic in the Detention Unit, and I'm sure we will be able to proceed on Monday. We will be prepared to cross-examine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I do not also think that there was any hope that we could finish with this witness this -- today, so you are not terribly inconvenienced. You are still going to be here next Monday anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then the matter then stands adjourned to next Monday at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in this same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.44 p.m.,
